newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kuehbacher seeks automatic EMU fiscal sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Kuehbacher seeks automatic EMU fiscal sanctions.

text.p: German Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said in a speech on Friday that a stability pact without automatic sanctions to control fiscal overshooting would not protect the stability of European currency union.
"Stability threatening developments have to be avoided. A stability pact without automatic sanctions to protect against fiscal inefficiency cannot be left out," Kuehbacher said.
Kuehbacher, president of the central bank of Berlin and Brandenburg, went on to say that if markets doubted EMU stability, then this could cause major market turbulence.

"If investors' trust in the money markets is let down, and if international financial markets doubt the price stability of currency union, then we can reckon with a high level of turbulence on the capital markets before January 1, 1999," said Kuehbacher in a speech to be given in Braunschweig.
Germany's call for automatic sanctions against fiscal overshooting inside EMU has been met with scepticism by other EU members who prefer a political control mechanism.

There were hints from officials at the Dublin summit on Friday that the summit was likely to endorse a compromise that would fall well short of Germany's original demands for automatic fines on budget offenders.
While the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union does allow for leeway on the criteria for fiscal convergence, Kuehbacher said that on no account could monetary union be allowed to start "at any price".
Kuehbacher said turbulence on the capital markets could only be avoided if European governments and central banks insisted on a strict adherence to the Maastricht criteria.

Countries wishing to join monetary union must be economically fit and demonstrate a high level of homegeneity, and the Maastricht Treaty contains criteria for measuring the economic fitness of a member state.
"Only those countries who can conclusively prove their long-term stability should be allowed take part in currency union," Kuehbacher said.

There were fears among European partners that the Bundesbank would occupy too strong a role in currency union, given its current dominance in deciding the course of European monetary and currency policy.

"To this end it is understandable that other European countries, especially France, want monetary policy authority to be transferred to a European body, in which they also have a say," said Kuehbacher.
